name: Procurement language for platform-neutral access requirements
consequences: Direct effect: Procurement documents will require non-Apple/Google trust anchors and fallback paths, reducing single-vendor dependency. Downstream implication: this creates negotiation overhead and potential delays in procurement while broadening supplier options and regulatory clarity.
options: Embed platform-neutral authentication requirements into all future Digitaliseringsstyrelsen procurements, mandating fallback access paths and standards-based credentials that do not depend on Apple or Google signals.
Create a staged procurement framework that permits interim pilots of platform-neutral fallback components while establishing long-term neutrality criteria across supplier contracts.
Publish an open standards blueprint showing compliance with NSIS and eIDAS for platform-neutral access to guide supplier responses and regulator reviews.
review: Trade-off: it redirects focus to procurement mechanics and vendor negotiations, potentially delaying deployment; the gap is the lack of concrete enforcement mechanisms and measurable milestones across phase transitions within the three options.

name: Fallback demonstrators to prove viability
consequences: Direct effect: Demonstrators provide concrete evidence for platform-neutral fallback viability outside MitID. Downstream implication: phase-two scope may face funding and political support constraints, limiting validity for production deployments.
options: Develop phase-two non-production demonstrators using WebAuthn/OpenID Connect on GrapheneOS to demonstrate platform-neutral access in a controlled environment.
Create a browser-based or hardware-token fallback prototype that bypasses mobile OS trust signals to build credible evidence for procurement and standards alignment.
Coordinate independent security reviews and publish demonstrator results to build trust with Digitaliseringsstyrelsen and EU authorities.
review: Trade-off: demonstrator focus may not translate into production-grade interoperability, risking overconfidence; the gap is absence of a clear path to scale from non-production demos to procurement-ready requirements.

name: EU standards alignment and advocacy for AltID
consequences: Direct effect: EU engagement may gradually shape Danish procurement language and AltID guidance; Downstream implication: domestic progress could stall if EU processes move slowly or conflict with national timelines.
options: Engage EU working groups to push platform-neutral language into European Digital Identity Wallet materials, aligning Danish goals with shared standards.
Submit formal proposals to EU bodies to include fallback authentication requirements in AltID guidance and procurement rules.
Coordinate with Danish researchers to publish joint position papers framing platform-neutral access as resilience and continuity imperative.
review: Trade-off: EU alignment can slow domestic progress if external processes take precedence; the gap is uncertainty about binding effects on Danish procurement timelines and the speed of market responses.

name: Standards-driven architecture for platform neutrality
consequences: Direct effect: Standards-focused work builds credibility for platform-neutral access; Downstream implication: increased technical complexity and longer lead times for consensus among stakeholders.
options: Advocate for inclusion of FIDO2/WebAuthn and OpenID Connect as core standards in AltID interoperability tests, emphasizing device-agnostic authentication.
Commission a technical shadow architecture mapping how a platform-neutral fallback would integrate with NSIS and eIDAS in practice, without altering MitID core.
Collaborate with privacy-preserving platform partners to validate cross-platform telemetry controls within a fallback path to reduce vendor lock-in.
review: Trade-off: technical complexity and standards adoption may delay concrete contracts; the gap is lacking a concrete plan for maintaining security guarantees during transition and ensuring ongoing MitID compatibility.

name: Procurement governance for resilience and continuity
consequences: Direct effect: governance measures reduce concentration risk; Downstream implication: added administrative overhead and potential friction with existing suppliers.
options: Create continuity clauses in procurement with supplier-diversity requirements and explicit fallback commitments for critical authentication workloads.
Institute periodic security and resilience reviews across identity procurement contracts to detect over-reliance on any single platform signal.
Establish a governance forum including civil society, academia, and procurement authorities to coordinate ongoing pressure for platform neutrality.
review: Trade-off: governance overhead may bog down decision-making; the gap is absence of explicit enforcement levers, milestones, and remedy pathways if continuity commitments are not met.

name: Coalition-building for resilience and accountability
consequences: Direct effect: coalition work increases political pressure and visibility; Downstream implication: risk of politicization or dilution if messaging diverges among stakeholders.
options: Form a broad coalition with civil society, privacy advocates, and parliamentary committees to articulate a platform-neutral risk narrative and demand procurement neutrality.
Publish accessible briefing materials that translate technical risk into resilience benefits for policymakers and the public.
Coordinate with media and academic partners to monitor and publicly report progress against milestones, keeping pressure on the vendor status quo.
review: Trade-off: public scrutiny could become a distraction or politicize decisions; the gap is a lack of a unified, binding action plan that translates coalition statements into procurement language.

name: AltID fallback-path governance and procurement alignment
consequences: Direct effect: formalizes platform-neutral fallback requirements within AltID procurement, reducing reliance on a single ecosystem. Downstream: procurement cycles become more complex, and external vendors gain clearer competition lanes, but certification timelines and EU alignment remain potential bottlenecks.
options: Publish platform-neutral fallback requirements in AltID procurement language, anchored in OpenID Connect and FIDO2 criteria demonstrated in phase two.
Establish an independent validation gate to test fallback readiness against MitID dependency surfaces before any live deployment.
Pilot a dedicated procurement track for fallback solutions separate from core MitID vendors to reduce cross-dependency risk.
review: Trade-off: formalizing platform-neutral procurement slows cycle times, potentially delaying rollout; the options leave unaddressed how to accelerate EU-level certification or enforce cross-agency adoption.

name: NSIS-aligned interoperability blueprint for platform neutrality
consequences: Direct effect: creates NSIS-aligned interoperability milestones and reference implementations that reduce platform lock-in. Downstream: vendors must adopt NSIS-compatible APIs, which may extend initial integration timelines but improve cross-border portability and future-proofing.
options: Develop a phased interoperability blueprint aligning AltID with NSIS and eIDAS2 signals, including test harnesses and milestone-based evaluations.
Commission an external NSIS-compliance review with concrete gaps and remediation plans, tied to phase milestones.
Pilot NSIS-compatible wallet integrations across two pilot services to de-risk cross-border acceptance and promote vendor competition.
review: Trade-off: standards alignment adds integration overhead and can slow onboarding; gap: the options do not specify how to measure interoperability in practice or enforce timely compliance.

name: Open standards demonstrators for platform independence
consequences: Direct effect: two non-production demonstrators validate that secure, standards-based fallback access is feasible without platform lock-in. Downstream: this expands Phase Two scope and resource needs but strengthens policy leverage for procurement discussions.
options: Build two non-production demonstrators using WebAuthn and OpenID Connect on GrapheneOS with browser-based fallback capabilities to test end-to-end scenarios.
Institute a parallel hardware-token-based fallback demonstrator to reduce OS-level dependency and improve portability across devices.
Develop a transparent demonstration report with security assumptions and risk tracking to inform procurement discussions.
review: Trade-off: broad demonstrator scope diverts resources and may slow other deliverables; gap: the options do not specify how to translate demonstrator outcomes into binding procurement requirements.

name: Supplier-diversification and resilience requirements in procurement
consequences: Direct effect: expands supplier base and forces competition, lowering concentration risk. Downstream: increased negotiation complexity and potential cost penalties, but resilience improves.
options: Require split-contracts for fallback components with independent testing and separate SLAs to prevent a single failure point.
Create a staged onboarding schedule that limits dependency on any single vendor and spreads risk across alternate providers.
Establish a transparency framework that publicly documents supplier concentration metrics and mitigation plans to inform audits.
review: Trade-off: diversification increases coordination overhead and risk of fragmented implementation; gap: lacks specified concentration thresholds or enforcement mechanisms.

name: EU-aligned advocacy and standards engagement for platform neutrality
consequences: Direct effect: elevates platform-neutrality as a political objective in EU policy and standards discussions, improving leverage for Denmark. Downstream: progress depends on political dynamics and cross-border consensus, which can be slow.
options: Submit a formal EU-aligned policy brief advocating platform-neutral fallback paths and required interoperability standards to relevant Digital Identity forums.
Coordinate with EU working groups to draft a shared interoperability charter binding member states to minimum NSIS-compatible requirements.
Organize a cross-border stakeholder workshop with privacy advocates and regulators to test compliance concepts and gather feedback.
review: Trade-off: EU advocacy diverts focus from national procurement gains; gap: options do not specify how to translate EU positions into binding procurement terms within Danish timelines.

name: Continuity-of-service resilience drills and incident response planning
consequences: Direct effect: introduces practice-oriented risk testing and formal incident response planning. Downstream: requires scheduled exercises and defined data-access controls, but strengthens readiness against platform-policy shifts.
options: Schedule quarterly resilience drills simulating platform-policy disruptions and verify fallback authentication effectiveness under governance constraints.
Develop a cross-institution incident-response playbook that standardizes notifications, escalation, and recovery steps for fallback pathways.
Publish a continuous-risk monitoring framework with metrics and triggers to maintain procurement readiness for platform-neutral access.
review: Trade-off: drills consume time and budget, may surface gaps requiring reallocation; gap: the options do not specify how drill outputs translate into binding procurement-ready requirements or vendor-specific action plans.

name: Fallback authentication pathway validation
consequences: Shifting emphasis toward validating a platform-neutral fallback pathway strengthens resilience by reducing reliance on platform-integrity signals. Downstream, procurement and standards teams must align OpenID Connect, WebAuthn, and GrapheneOS demonstrations across Phase two (months 9–16) to Phase three (months 17–24), potentially delaying production-readiness milestones.
options: Establish a platform-neutral fallback architecture by mapping existing MitID dependencies and defining compliance criteria for OpenID Connect and WebAuthn.
Develop a standards-based reference implementation on GrapheneOS and OpenID Connect to demonstrate practical fallback authentication under phased testing.
Engage Digitaliseringsstyrelsen and the MitID operator to codify fallback-path requirements into Phase three procurement and interoperability standards.
review: Trade-off centers on aligning fallback validation with existing MitID trust anchors; the options leave unaddressed whether non-production demonstrators can scale to real-world access without live MitID integration.

name: NSIS and EU wallet interoperability pressure
consequences: Pursuing NSIS and EU wallet interoperability pressure aligns Denmark with European resilience goals but may slow national procurement adjustments to cater to domestic timelines. Downstream, the effort can compromise speed of concrete supplier diversification actions if EU timelines override Danish decision gates.
options: Lobby EU bodies and NSIS working groups to recognize platform-neutral fallback as essential for resilience and portability in the AltID roadmap.
Publish a formal crosswalk document mapping NSIS signals to Danish fallback authentication requirements to speed regulatory alignment.
Coordinate with Danish stakeholders to align procurement language with EU wallet interoperability expectations for level Substantial or higher.
review: Trade-off centers on policy alignment versus national procurement agility; the options may not secure timely domestic procurement protections if EU timelines dominate.

name: Coalition-driven procurement leverage
consequences: Trade-off centers on political leverage versus risk of diluting focus; the options may not secure concrete decision gates fast enough to influence Phase two milestones.
options: Establish a civil-society and academic coalition that actively feeds procurement negotiations with data on resilience and supplier concentration risk.
Deploy a formal stakeholder matrix with lead times and blockers, enabling faster decision gates during phase two and three.
Organize alternating roundtables with Folketinget's digital policy committee to maintain political momentum without prescriptive commitments.
review: The coalition approach gains legitimacy but may diffuse focus; the options do not guarantee timely gate approvals or firm commitments from key agencies.

name: Public-sector risk disclosure and transparency drive
consequences: Shifting toward public-sector risk disclosure improves accountability but can reveal vulnerabilities early in the process. Downstream, the three options may still fall short of delivering binding procurement protections or commitments from key agencies.
options: Publish a risk register and dependency surface mapping, highlighting platform concentration exposure to inform procurement risk assessments.
Institute quarterly public briefings detailing milestones, blockers, and regulatory friction to sustain accountability and external scrutiny.
Develop a red-teaming exercise with independent security researchers to expose procurement and architecture gaps without exposing sensitive data.
review: Transparency drives legitimacy but can trigger resistance; the options do not ensure binding protections from agencies that resist changing current practices.

name: Independent demonstrator consortium for platform-neutral access
consequences: Trade-off: independent demonstrators enable credible testing but may lack official authority; the options leave unaddressed how results secure formal adoption or procurement leverage.
options: Coordinate a non-production demonstrator consortium to compare WebAuthn, FIDO2, and OpenID approaches across multiple device platforms.
Publish open testing harness and evaluation criteria for fallback candidates to invite external validation and independent scoring.
Secure commitments from a Danish university and security-qualified R&D facility for ongoing demonstrator maintenance across phase two.
review: Independent demonstrations boost credibility but risk lacking official mandate; the options do not guarantee formal adoption or procurement leverage signals.

name: EU wallet alignment advocacy and pilots
consequences: Advocating EU wallet alignment supports national interoperability goals but may compress room for flexible national procurement experiments. Downstream, the options may leave unaddressed the risk that EU deliberations outpace Danish procurement cycles, delaying concrete changes in AltID-related procurement documents.
options: Submit a position paper advocating platform-neutral access and certified fallback mechanisms to EU Digital Identity Wallet working groups.
Coordinate pilot proposals with EU member states to test interoperability of fallback authentication in national contexts.
Develop a policy dialogue with EU regulators to align national procurement language with wallet interoperability and resilience provisions.
review: EU-level advocacy may slow domestic action; the options do not guarantee timely translation of EU talks into concrete Danish procurement changes.
